2. Rules were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, should not be declared void, illegal, ultra vires the Constitution and are of no legal effect and as to why the Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10(10)/1996 dated 2-10-96 and Lalbagh PS Case No. 11 (11)/5 dated 4-11-75 should not be declared illegal, unlawful and void. 

 22. It is submitted that though Martial Law was promulgated all over the country, yet the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh remained in force side by side, only subject to the provisions of the Martial Law Proclamations, Regulations and Orders. This Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 was promulgated by Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed as President of this country in exercise of this power conferred by Clause (1) of Article 93 of the Constitution as the Parliament was then not in session. Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed did not promulgate that law as a Martial Law Administrator, or that law was neither a Martial Law Proclamation nor a Regulation nor an Order. Usurping the power of the President of Bangladesh Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed promulgated the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 under Article 93(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh. Since the Constitution was in force, this Court should consider as to whether that Ordinance was promulgated in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. This Ordinance was not made a part of the Constitution. If that Ordinance infringes any provisions of the Constitution, then it would be ultra vires of the Constitution. If any law is found ultra vires of the Constitution, that law cannot be saved by the Constitution itself inasmuch as a void law repugnant to the Constitution cannot be saved by or under any other law. 

 7(2) "This Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people, the supreme law of the Republic, and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution, that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void." 

 "The State shall not make any law inconsistent with any provision of this Part, and any law so made shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void." 

 24. Learned Attorney-General submits that under Article 93(1) of the Constitution the President is competent to promulgate Ordinance, but such Ordinance will take effect from the date of its promulgation. In the instant cases occurrence took place on 15-8-1975, but the Ordinance was promulgated on 26-9-1975. Such a subsequent Ordinance could not be given retrospective effect from 15-8-75 inasmuch as the effect of this Ordinance will take place on the very day of its promulgation, that is, on 26-9-75. Since this Ordinance was not in force on 16-8-75 and since retrospective effect has been given to it, it offends Article 93(1) of the Constitution and, as such, it is void. He further submits that the Ordinance No.50 of 1975 provided something which could not be provided by the Parliament itself and, as such, it offends Article 93(1)(i) of the Constitution. 

 26. Mr. Attorney-General submits that these Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution are fundamental human rights guaranteed by our Constitution. So, right to life and body is protected under the fundamental rights which cannot be taken away except in accordance with law. On the fateful day, that is, 15-8-1975 the lives of the then President Bangabandhu Shaikh Mujibur Rahman and his family members and others were taken away by a group of army people without any sanction of law. In our ordinary laws, namely, the Penal Code or Army Act and in some other laws life of a person can be taken away by holding a trial in accordance with law. But in the morning of 15th August, 1975, the President along with his family members and others were killed by some army people and such an action of taking away life was not permitted by any law. If any person takes away life of another person, he must be tried in accordance with the existing law of the land. This Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 put restriction on taking any legal proceeding against the killers and though they committed the offence of murder, they were made immune from being tried under the ordinary laws of the land. Since the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 has made provision for not trying the army people or any person who committed murder, for which the normal law was in force for trial, such an Ordinance, in fact, offends Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution inasmuch as, although without any sanction of law the President and his family members were killed, the killers were given protection by the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. Though the killers were liable for trial under ordinary laws of the land for killing several persons as stated above, by promulgating such Ordinance the killers were made impugned from facing the trial under the laws of the land. So, this Ordinance, in fact, offends and infringes the provisions of Articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution and, as such, the Indemnity Ordinance is void being ultra vires the Constitution. 

 28. Learned Attorney-General submits that this Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 does not come within the purview of the above Article 46 of the Constitution. Since this Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was contrary to the provisions of Article 46 of the Constitution, the entire Ordinance was ultra vires of the Constitution, that is, the said Ordinance offended Article 46 of the Constitution. As such, it was void ab-initio. Since the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 itself was ultra vires the Constitution and void ab-initio, neither the Indemnity Ordinance itself was protected nor the results, consequence, effect, benefit or alleged vested right are saved under paragraph 3A and paragraph 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. 

 30. Mr. Korban Ali submits that the Ordinance or the Act might be repealed by subsequent amendment, but the consequence, result, benefit or any rights accrued out of the same will be saved under section 6 of the General Clauses Act, and in the instant cases, the same were saved under section 6 of the said Act and under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. General Clauses Act is applicable to the provisions of this Constitution vide Article 152(2) of the Constitution. But Mr. Attorney-General submits that since the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 was ultra vires the Constitution and void ab-initio, it cannot be saved by the Constitution itself inasmuch as the law in question offended its own provisions. Not only the Ordinance, but even any right, privilege, benefit, consequence or result accorded under the said Ordinance also could not be protected by paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution in view of the fact that a void law cannot create any result, consequence, benefit or legal or vested right to a person. A void law is non-existent from its very birth and if a law is void, it will never create any right or benefit or privilege in favour of a person for whom it is made, A void law does not exist in the statute book or in the Constitution as a law. 

 37. Learned Attorney-General submits that if a law is ultra vires the Constitution and is void ab-initio, the jurisdiction of the Court can never be barred to see the validity of a void law. Learned Attorney-General has referred to Law Lexicon showing different meanings of the words void and ultra vires. Referring to the case of TB Co-operative Society vs. Chief Commissioner of Monipur, AIR 1969 (Mori.) 84, he submits that void means the judgment which defaulted as one which has no legal force or effect. He further submits that void means non-existent from its very inception and a ban against its recognition. In substance and in effect there is no difference between any Act which is repealed or an Act which is declared void. In both cases the Act ceases to be operative. He relies on the case of State of Bombay vs. Homan Shantolal, AIR 1952 (Bom) 16. This word, that is, 'void' is to be interpreted to mean that such a law is void from its very commencement. Even in juristic writing expression void and ultra vires are used in different sense. A thing that is void in the strict sense of the word is merely a nullity and may be ignored even in collateral proceeding as it never were. Void ab-initio is the expression Court often used to take. The expression ultra vires strictly implies to an absence of the jurisdiction as well as the absence of the competency. The word void in its strict sense for all practical purposes is non-est and may be ignored in collateral proceeding as found in the case of Madhavan Pillai vs. State of Kerala, AIR 1966 (Kera) 212. 

 38. In the case of Chowdhury Mainuddin vs. Deputy Director, Military Land and Cantonment, AIR 1956 (All.) 684, it was held that where a law is void, it has no existence in the eye of law and, as such, it is a nullity and may be ignored altogether. It was further held that an unconstitutional Act is not a law, it confers no right; it imposes no duties; it affords no protection; it creates no office; it is in illegal contemplation as inoperative as if it had never been passed. Contract purporting to be made by statutory corporation or companies which are outside the power conferred by statute or taken by the Memorandum of Association are ultra vires and void and no ratification by all or any of the members can make them valid. In this connection the learned Attorney-General has also referred to the case of P. Janardhana Shetty vs. Union of India, AIR 1970 (Mysore) 171. 

 39. Learned Attorney-General submits that since the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was ultra vires the Constitution and was void ab-initio, such a void statute cannot be protected under Paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. He further submits that since the Indemnity Ordinance was ultra vires the Constitution and void ab-initio, it did not create any legal or vested right, benefit and legal consequence in favour of the killers who killed the then President Bangabandhu Shaikh Mujibur Rahman and his family members and others. As the instant Act, namely, Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 repealed the void Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 and has undone all its effects, consequences and results, this Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 did not offend or infringe any provision of the Constitution by repealing a void Ordinance. It is a settled principle that a void law can never create any right or obligation in favour of any person for whom it is made. Substance of learned Attorney-General's submission is that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, is ultra vires the provisions of Articles 27, 31, 32, 46, 62 and 93(1)(i) of the Constitution and the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, is a valid legislation which does not offend any provision of the Constitution. 

 40. Six senior learned members of the Bar were requested by this Court to assist it as Amicus Curiae. Amongst them, Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, former Attorney-General for Bangladesh and a renowned jurist, submits that the indemnity can be given in a very limited way under Article 46 of the Constitution. Since the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 does not come within the purview of Article 46 of the Constitution, it is a nullity and void and it was done or passed in contravention of the provisions of Article 46 of the Constitution. The Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 offended also fundamental right No. 27 of the Constitution. Article 27 of the Constitution runs as follows: 

 44. Mr. Rafiqul Huq further submits that the law, namely, the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 was passed in order to remove the barrier for prosecuting and punishing the persons who committed crime against humanity on 15th August, 1975. To challenge such a law means to obstruct the trial and punishment of the persons who committed offence against humanity and, as such, the present writ petitions are not maintainable in view of the provisions of Article 47 A(2) of the Constitution which provides that notwithstanding anything contained in this Constitution no person to whom a law applicable to clause (3) of Article 47 shall have the right to move the Supreme Court for any of the remedies under the Constitution. He further submits that Article 47(a)(1) provides that the right guaranteed under Article 41, clauses (1) and (3) of the Articles 35 and 44 shall not apply to any person to whom a law specified in clause (3) of Article 47 applies. Article 47(3) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in this Constitution, no law nor any' provision thereof providing for detention, prosecution or punishment of any person, who is a member of any armed or defence or auxiliary forces or who is a prisoner of war, for genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes and other crimes under international law, shall be deemed void or unlawful, or ever to have become void or unlawful, on the ground that such law or provision of any such law is inconsistent with, or repugnant to, the provisions of this Constitution. Since the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, as a law, in fact, immuned the murderers from being tried for offence and crime against humanity, this law, in fact, was ultra vires of the provisions of the Article 47(3) of the Constitution of Bangladesh. 

 45. Dr. Kamal Hossain, another Amicus Curiae, and a renowned jurist, submits that the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 was not authorised under Article 46 of the Constitution and, as such, it was ultra vires of that Article. He further submits that no retrospective effect could be given to this Indemnify Ordinance, 1975, as the said law was not in force on 15-8-1975. No law can be promulgated to indemnify a person who took away the lives of several other persons including the President of Bangladesh on 15-8-1975. Such an Ordinance was ultra vires of Articles 27, 31 and 32 of the Constitution. Since the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was ultra vires of the Constitution and since it was no law in view of the provisions of the Constitution, paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution cannot protect and save a void law. No law can be promulgated providing that the murderers/ killers of human beings shall not be tried and punished though actually they committed the offence of murdering the President and his family members. Such a law itself is ultra vires of the Constitution infringing the fundamental right Nos. 27, 31 and 32 of the Constitution. 

 46. Dr Kamal Hossain summarises his submissions in the following manner that Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was not a law in the eye of the Constitution. Since it was repugnant to the Constitution it was void ab-initio. There can be no law of indemnity except as provided under Article 46 of the Constitution. Concept of indemnity is very limited even in times of war. Paragraph 3A(7) of the 4th Schedule and Article 149 of the Constitution provide for amendment and repeal of the Acts or Ordinance and, as such, the question of declaring the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 void or ultra vires the Constitution does not arise at all. He further submits that the views expressed in Dosso's case, 11 DLR (SC) 1, in fact, were buried by the decision given in Asma Jilani's case, viz. Asma Jilani vs. Government of Punjab, PLD 1972 (SC) 139. 

 48. Mr. M. Nurullah further submits that since Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was ultra vires of the Constitution and void ab-initio it cannot stand the test of an existing and continuing law and, as such, such a void law cannot get protection under Paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution inasmuch as a void law has no legal existence and it should be presumed that there exists no law in the eye of the Constitution. It was born dead and had no legal existence. 

 49. He further submits that the jurisdiction of the Court has also been barred by paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution, but well-settled principle is this, that even if there is ouster of jurisdiction of the Court, the Court can look into it as to whether there was actual ouster of jurisdiction and as to how far the ouster clause can be extended. So, if a law is ultra vires the Constitution and void, the High Court Division can definitely examine and look into the matter under Article 102 of the Constitution in view of the fact that even if there is ouster of jurisdiction of Court, even by Martial Law Proclamation or Regulation, the Court can exercise its jurisdiction to look into it if there is a question of without jurisdiction, coram non judiceor malafide. In this connection he has referred to the cases of Khondker Ehtesham Uddin Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 provides that the certificate can be given by the President or any other authorised person on his behalf and it will be sufficient evidence of such Act. It does not say that the alleged certificate would be conclusive evidence. Since the restriction was put on the trial of some acts and since the alleged certificate would be taken as sufficient evidence, he submits, the scope of trying the offenders by the Court was still open even without repealing the said Ordinance No. 50 of 1973 inasmuch as there was no total prohibition of trying the offenders and the alleged certificate could not be a conclusive evidence of such an offence. By specific language the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996, has taken away all the effects and consequences of the so-called Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, and, as such, there is no scope to challenge this Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 as this Act of Parliament does not infringe any provision of the Constitution. Rather the power of repealing such an Ordinance by the appropriate authority has been conferred under paragraph No. 3A(7) of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution and, as such, there is no scope to challenge it on the ground of unconstitutionality. 

 50. Mr. M Amirul Islam, another learned Amicus Curiae and a renowned jurist, submits that it is the guiding principle of our Constitution that there is Constitutional supremacy and rule of law. He submits that only under Article 46 of the Constitution the indemnity can be granted to those persons as prescribed by Article 46 itself and not beyond that. This Article 46 is an exception in the Constitution. It has got two parts, one substantive part and another procedural part. Indemnify Ordinance, 1975, on the face of it, does not come within the purview of Article 46 of the Constitution. He further submits that only Parliament can make a law to indemnify a person as contemplated under Article 46 of the Constitution, but not by way of promulgating an Ordinance under Article 93(1) of the Constitution. As such, this Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, being not within the purview of Article 46 of the Constitution, cannot be called an Ordinance in the eye of law as it offends Article 46 of the Constitution. Further, this Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 offends Articles 27, 31 and 32 of the Constitution and, as such, the same was void ab-initio, It is further submitted that Khondaker Moshtaque Ahmed usurped the power by virtue of a military coup detat and not by any revolution or under any Constitutional process. With the help of a few army people he killed the then President of this country and his family members, and usurped the power of the country. He was nothing but a de facto unconstitutional Ruler. Since he usurped the power in unconstitutional manner, he cannot be called a source of law or law giver and if any law is given by him, it cannot be called a law in the eye of the Constitution. De facto dictator cannot be a source of law. 

 55. Mr. Amirul Islam further submits that if any void law exists, then remedy lies in two ways in order to avoid that void law. It should be done either by a Court declaring the law void or it must be repealed by a declaratory statute. In the instant case though the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, was void ab-initio, it never came before the Court for any declaration like that and, as such, it was running in the statute book as an existing law. The Parliament in its wisdom thought that it is a void law and, as such, it passed the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 repealing the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975. So, validity of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 cannot be questioned in any manner whatsoever. 

 69. Learned Attorney General and the five learned Amicus Curiae expressed the view that since the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was void being ultra vires the Constitution, it was void ab-initio and in the eye of the Constitution there existed no law like the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. They further submit that Indemnity Ordinance was born dead and it had no legal existence from its birth. Since the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, was void being ultra vires the Constitution, it cannot be considered as one of the 'other laws' as referred to in paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. Since the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, was void ab-initio, it had no legal existence on 26th of September, 1975 and, as such, it can neither be a part of the Constitution nor it can be one of the existing 'other laws" as provided under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule of the Constitution. So, it appears to us that a void law though not declared void by any Court so long was legally repealed by the Parliament and, as such, there was no illegality or unconstitutionality in passing the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996. 

 70. As regards ouster of jurisdiction arguments have been advanced by the learned Advocates stating that even if in the Martial Law Proclamation or Regulation there was ouster clause, even then our Appellate Division had decided in so many cases that this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution.is competent to see as to whether there was actual ouster of jurisdiction or not and also as to what is the extent and scope of such ouster clause. As in the instant case the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, is found void ab-initio being ultra vires the Constitution, this Court has got the jurisdiction to consider the constitutionality of such a law. 

 "Thus, the particular phraseology of the Constitution of the United States confirms and strengthens the principle, supposed to be essential to all written Constitutions, that a law repugnant to the Constitution is void and that Courts, as well as other departments, are bound by that instrument" 

 72. Towards the close of his submissions Mr. Attorney-General referred to the celebrated decision given in the case of Miss Benazir Bhutto vs. Federation of Pakistan, PLD 1988 (SC) 416. Eleven Judges of the Pakistan Supreme Court heard the case for eleven days and then passed this big judgment. From the above decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court we may got substantial support in the instant cases. Some amendments were made in Political Parties Act of 1962 during Martial Law providing for compulsory registration of political parties. Challenging such amendments made by the Martial Law Authority and ultimately protected, preserved, ratified and confirmed in the Constitution, Benazir Bhutta moved the Supreme Court, thereupon the Supreme Court of Pakistan gave the above judgment declaring section 3- B of the Political Parties Act, 1962, void in its entirety. 

 73. Answer to the question of ouster of jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. High Court Division, under Article 102 of the Constitution, is hidden in the judgment of the case of Khandkar Moshtaque Ahmed vs. Bangladesh, 34 DLR (AD) 222 where the learned Amicus Curiae Mr. Khondker himself appeared. In that judgment our Appellate Division declared the entire trial of Khondker Moshtaque Ahmed under Martial Law Regulation void and without jurisdiction on the ground of malafide. So, from the above judgment it appears to us that any act or thing done or any trial taken place even under Martial Law Proclamation, Regulation or Order, can be challenged under Article 102 of the Constitution if it is done or made without jurisdiction, coram non judice or malafide. 

 78. He further submits that this Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 was an ex-post facto legislation by which benefit or right can be given retrospectively, but no provision can be made for punishing a person retrospectively which was not a punishment at the time of promulgation of Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. By ex-post facto legislation the vested right of the persons who were connected with 15th August, 1975, incident, cannot be taken away. This theory of ex post facto legislation is not tenable in the instant case in view of the fact that the Indemnity Ordinance of 1975 appears to be void being ultra vires of the Constitution. Agreeing with the decision reported in AIR 1956 (All) 684, we also hold that an unconstitutional Act is not a law: it confers no right; it imposes no duties; it affords no protection; it creates no office; it is, in legal contemplation as inoperative as if it has never been passed. 

 85. With regard to the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975, the Respondents advanced two-fold arguments. Firstly, Constitution was in force with the proclamation of Martial Law on 20th August, 1975, and when Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 was promulgated on 26-9-75, it offended Articles 46, 27, 31, 32, 62 and 93(1)(i) of the Constitution and, as such, it was void under Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution. Secondly, it was not brought to judicial scrutiny at any time before and with the withdrawal of Martial Law the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 was saved and protected under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the 4th Schedule as existing law within the category of "Other Laws". So, this Ordinance No.50 of 1975, is repugnant to the Constitution offending its Articles 46, 27, 31, 32, 62 and 93(1)(i) and, as such, it is void under Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution. Considering the above we hold that the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 is ultra vires the Constitution and as such it is void under Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution. As we are declaring this Ordinance No.50 of 1975 void, it had and has no legal existence in the eye of the Constitution on the very day when it was promulgated that is on 26-9-75 and now. 

 86. As the Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 is declared void under Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution, it will not create any benefit, consequence, result or legal or vested right in favour of the persons for whom it was made and, as such, we hold that the benefit of section 6 of the General Clauses Act is not applicable to those persons who claim any benefit or legal right out of the said Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975. 

 87. As the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 repealed the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975, and as the petitioners, relying upon the provisions of the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975, have made prayers for declaring the institution of the two criminal cases viz, Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10(10) of 1996 and Lalbagh PS Case No. 11(11) of 1975 void, illegal and without jurisdiction, we had to see the constitutional validity of the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975. After due consideration of the provisions of the Constitution and Law, we hold that the prayers of the petitioners for declaring the above two criminal proceedings illegal, void and without jurisdiction cannot be accepted, because the very Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 itself is void being repugnant to the Constitution. 

 88. In this connection we like to refer to the famous sayings of MD Bidwas, a renowned Jurist, made in his book "Philosophy of Law" that "jurisprudence is said to be the daughter of philosophy. Every law must have its own philosophy. But a legal philosophy devoid of moral quality, if based purely on legal relations, may ultimately reduce the terms to be related to a cipher. This skeleton of legal relations may so dominate over the members of the social order that they vanish altogether. So the social order must be "good" one and one in which both the individual and the community are properly balanced and harmonised. 

 89. For this point of view the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, attained a technical status of law because of ratification by the Constitution (5th Amendment) Act, 1979, but being against nature and natural justice cannot be law in the true sense of the term. Besides, this being repugnant to our Constitution cannot be a law and is void. 

 (3) It is held that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 (Ordinance No. 50 of 1975) is void since it is repugnant to the Constitution. 

 (5) It is found that five out of six learned Jurists of the country (excepting Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed) who assisted the Court as Amicus Curiae, expressed their views that the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 is a valid piece of legislation and the Indemnity Ordinance, No. 50 of 1975 is void being ultra vires the Constitution. Submissions of the learned Attorney-General and the views of the majority Amicus Curiae on the points of validity of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No. 21 of 1996 and the repugnancy of the Indemnity Ordinance No. 50 of 1975 appear to be constitutionally and legally correct and, as such, the same are accepted.
